title: Write a custom indicator in JavaScript
summary: Learn the code structure, inputs and outputs, parameters, and line styles of a JavaScript indicator, then build one from three working examples.
outcome: You will write a JavaScript indicator that appears on the chart and know its limits and what its error messages mean.
before: Know some JavaScript: variables, arrays, for loops, and functions.
Write common standard indicators as TDX formulas first; use JavaScript for logic a TDX formula cannot express.

sections.title: 1. Three things that are different
sections.body:
The editor accepts standard JavaScript syntax, run in an isolated sandbox. Compared with code for a web page or Node, three things are different:

  1. The whole source is one object. Its first character must be { or (. Do not write export default or module.exports, and do not start with a comment, or the editor reads the code as a TDX formula.
  2. The sandbox has plain JavaScript only. There is no window or document, no network, no require or import for libraries, and no timers. console.log prints nothing.
  3. There are no built-in MA, EMA, or STD functions. Write the calculations yourself with arrays and loops.

Modern syntax works: let, const, arrow functions, destructuring, template strings, ?. and ??, class, Map, Set, Math, and JSON.

steps.title: Open custom indicators
steps.body: Go to Strategy → Indicators, switch to Custom at the top left, and click + to create a custom indicator.

steps.title: Paste the code
steps.body: Delete the default TDX formula in the editor and paste your JavaScript. Indicator name can stay empty. With Display position set to Auto detect, overlay in your code decides between the main chart and a subplot.

steps.title: Save and add it to a chart
steps.body: Saving checks the syntax and structure. After saving, the indicator appears in the chart’s Add indicator menu.

sections.title: 3. Code structure
sections.body:
Paste and save this first. If a close-price line appears in a subplot, everything is set up; then add your own calculation.

{
  name: 'Close price',
  params: [],
  lines: [
    { name: 'CLOSE', defaultColor: '#2962ff', defaultWidth: 1 }
  ],
  compute(candles, params) {
    return {
      lines: [
        { name: 'CLOSE', values: candles.map((c) => c.close) }
      ]
    }
  }
}
FieldRequiredDescription
nameYesIndicator name
shortNameNoShort name for the chart legend
overlayNotrue draws on the main chart; omitted or false draws in a subplot
paramsYesParameter list; write [] when there are none
linesYesLines to draw, at least one
subplotScaleNoSubplot axis, for example { min: 0, max: 100, levels: [30, 70] } fixes the range to 0–100 with horizontal lines at 30 and 70
computeYesThe calculation, compute(candles, params)

For shared helper functions, wrap the object in (() => { … return { … } })() and define the functions before return. Example 3 shows how.

sections.title: 4. What compute receives and returns
sections.body:
candles is an array of bars. Each bar has:

FieldDescription
timeBar time in Unix seconds (UTC)
open high low closeOpen, high, low, close
volumeVolume
oiOpen interest, for China futures only; undefined elsewhere
spreadSpread, when the data has it
  • Bars are ordered oldest first. The last one is the current bar at the replay cursor.
  • You receive a window of the chart timeframe, not the full history: about 3,000 bars before the cursor during playback, and up to about 33,000 when paused. Cumulative indicators such as OBV start counting at the first bar of the window.
  • params holds the current parameter values by id, for example params.period.

compute returns { lines: [{ name, values }] }:

  • Return the lines in the same order as the declared lines. The app matches them by position, not by name.
  • Each values array has candles.length items; item i belongs to bar i.
  • Use null where there is no value, and the line breaks there. A 4-period average, for example, starts with three null values.

sections.title: 5. Parameters
sections.body:
Each parameter becomes an input or a dropdown in the chart’s indicator settings, and its value reaches compute as params[id].

kindUseFields
'int'Whole numbers, such as a periodid label default, optional min max step
'float'Decimals, such as a multiplierSame as above
'source'Price source dropdownid label default, one of 'close' 'open' 'high' 'low' 'hl2' 'hlc3' 'ohlc4'
'select'Your own dropdownid label default options: [{ value, label }]

'source' only passes a string such as 'hl2'; your compute decides which price that means. Example 1 shows the code.

sections.title: 6. Line styles and other drawings
sections.body:

Besides lines, the result can include these drawings. Every index is a position in candles:

sections.title: 7. Example 1: Bollinger Bands
sections.body:
Draws three lines on the main chart, uses whole-number, decimal, and price-source parameters, and keeps rolling sums so the whole range is read once. The result matches Bollinger Bands written as a TDX formula in the app.

{
  name: 'Bollinger Bands (JS)',
  shortName: 'BOLL',
  overlay: true,
  params: [
    { kind: 'int', id: 'period', label: 'Period', default: 20, min: 2, max: 500 },
    { kind: 'float', id: 'mult', label: 'Multiplier', default: 2, min: 0.5, max: 5, step: 0.1 },
    { kind: 'source', id: 'src', label: 'Price', default: 'close' }
  ],
  lines: [
    { name: 'MID', defaultColor: '#f5a623', defaultWidth: 1 },
    { name: 'UPPER', defaultColor: '#2962ff', defaultWidth: 1 },
    { name: 'LOWER', defaultColor: '#2962ff', defaultWidth: 1 }
  ],

  compute(candles, params) {
    const n = Math.max(2, Math.round(params.period ?? 20))
    const k = Number(params.mult ?? 2)
    const len = candles.length

    // Pick the price once for the whole range
    const price = candles.map((c) => {
      switch (params.src) {
        case 'open': return c.open
        case 'high': return c.high
        case 'low': return c.low
        case 'hl2': return (c.high + c.low) / 2
        case 'hlc3': return (c.high + c.low + c.close) / 3
        case 'ohlc4': return (c.open + c.high + c.low + c.close) / 4
        default: return c.close
      }
    })

    const mid = new Array(len).fill(null)
    const upper = new Array(len).fill(null)
    const lower = new Array(len).fill(null)

    // Rolling sums: add the new bar, drop the oldest, one pass in total
    let sum = 0
    let sumSq = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      sum += price[i]
      sumSq += price[i] * price[i]
      if (i >= n) {
        sum -= price[i - n]
        sumSq -= price[i - n] * price[i - n]
      }
      if (i < n - 1) continue // fewer than n bars: leave null, nothing is drawn

      const mean = sum / n
      // Divides by n, like the app's TDX STD
      const sd = Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, sumSq / n - mean * mean))
      mid[i] = mean
      upper[i] = mean + k * sd
      lower[i] = mean - k * sd
    }

    // Same order as the lines declared above
    return {
      lines: [
        { name: 'MID', values: mid },
        { name: 'UPPER', values: upper },
        { name: 'LOWER', values: lower }
      ]
    }
  }
}

sections.title: 8. Example 2: RSI overbought and oversold
sections.body:
Draws in a subplot with a fixed 0–100 axis and lines at 30 and 70, and uses markers where RSI rises back above 30 or falls back below 70.

{
  name: 'RSI overbought/oversold (JS)',
  shortName: 'RSI',
  overlay: false,
  params: [
    { kind: 'int', id: 'period', label: 'Period', default: 14, min: 2, max: 200 }
  ],
  lines: [
    { name: 'RSI', defaultColor: '#7e57c2', defaultWidth: 2 }
  ],
  // Fixed 0-100 axis with horizontal lines at 30 and 70
  subplotScale: { min: 0, max: 100, levels: [30, 70] },

  compute(candles, params) {
    const n = Math.max(2, Math.round(params.period ?? 14))
    const rsi = new Array(candles.length).fill(null)
    const markers = []
    let avgGain = 0
    let avgLoss = 0

    for (let i = 1; i < candles.length; i++) {
      const change = candles[i].close - candles[i - 1].close
      const gain = Math.max(change, 0)
      const loss = Math.max(-change, 0)
      if (i <= n) {
        // First n bars: plain average gain and loss
        avgGain += gain / n
        avgLoss += loss / n
        if (i < n) continue
      } else {
        // After that: Wilder smoothing
        avgGain = (avgGain * (n - 1) + gain) / n
        avgLoss = (avgLoss * (n - 1) + loss) / n
      }
      rsi[i] = avgLoss === 0 ? 100 : 100 - 100 / (1 + avgGain / avgLoss)

      // Mark a rise back above 30 and a fall back below 70
      const prev = rsi[i - 1]
      if (prev !== null && prev < 30 && rsi[i] >= 30) {
        markers.push({ index: i, position: 'belowBar', shape: 'arrowUp', color: '#26a69a', text: 'Up' })
      }
      if (prev !== null && prev > 70 && rsi[i] <= 70) {
        markers.push({ index: i, position: 'aboveBar', shape: 'arrowDown', color: '#ef5350', text: 'Down' })
      }
    }

    return {
      lines: [{ name: 'RSI', values: rsi }],
      markers
    }
  }
}

sections.title: 9. Example 3: Moving average crossover
sections.body:
Wraps the object in (() => { … })() to define a shared sma function, and draws golden and death crosses as arrows with signal: true lines.

(() => {
  // Functions written before return can be used inside compute
  function sma(values, n) {
    const out = new Array(values.length).fill(null)
    let sum = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
      sum += values[i]
      if (i >= n) sum -= values[i - n]
      if (i >= n - 1) out[i] = sum / n
    }
    return out
  }

  return {
    name: 'MA crossover (JS)',
    shortName: 'MA CROSS',
    overlay: true,
    params: [
      { kind: 'int', id: 'fast', label: 'Fast', default: 10, min: 1, max: 500 },
      { kind: 'int', id: 'slow', label: 'Slow', default: 30, min: 2, max: 500 }
    ],
    lines: [
      { name: 'FAST', defaultColor: '#f5a623', defaultWidth: 1 },
      { name: 'SLOW', defaultColor: '#2962ff', defaultWidth: 2 },
      // A signal: true line draws arrows: positive values get an up arrow below
      // the bar, negative values a down arrow above it
      { name: 'Golden', defaultColor: '#26a69a', defaultWidth: 1, signal: true },
      { name: 'Death', defaultColor: '#ef5350', defaultWidth: 1, signal: true }
    ],

    compute(candles, params) {
      const close = candles.map((c) => c.close)
      const fast = sma(close, Math.max(1, Math.round(params.fast ?? 10)))
      const slow = sma(close, Math.max(2, Math.round(params.slow ?? 30)))
      const golden = new Array(close.length).fill(null)
      const death = new Array(close.length).fill(null)

      for (let i = 1; i < close.length; i++) {
        if ([fast[i - 1], slow[i - 1], fast[i], slow[i]].includes(null)) continue
        if (fast[i - 1] <= slow[i - 1] && fast[i] > slow[i]) golden[i] = 1
        if (fast[i - 1] >= slow[i - 1] && fast[i] < slow[i]) death[i] = -1
      }

      return {
        lines: [
          { name: 'FAST', values: fast },
          { name: 'SLOW', values: slow },
          { name: 'Golden', values: golden },
          { name: 'Death', values: death }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
})()

sections.title: 10. Limits
sections.body:
• Each calculation gets up to 2 seconds and 256 MB of memory. When it runs over or throws an error, the indicator shows nothing for that calculation, without a message.
  • The source can be up to 1 MB.
  • Every calculation starts in a fresh sandbox, so variables do not carry over between calculations.
  • JavaScript indicators draw on charts only. Trading-system rules and formula conditions under Strategy → Systems cannot reference them; write those indicators as TDX formulas.

callout.title: Keep the calculation fast
callout.body: The sandbox interprets your code, which is much slower than JavaScript in a browser, and playback recalculates the indicator on every new bar. Read the bars in a single pass where you can, as the rolling sums in Example 1 do, instead of looping N times for every bar. Several JavaScript indicators at once make playback stutter.

sections.title: 11. Error messages
sections.body:
Saving checks the syntax and structure and shows errors below the editor.

MessageCause
A TDX formula error, such as “no output line”The first character is not { or (: the code starts with a comment, export default, or module.exports
JavaScript indicator error: SyntaxError …A syntax error, such as an unmatched bracket or a missing comma
Missing name (string)name is missing
Missing compute() functionThere is no compute function
params must be an arrayparams is missing; write params: [] when there are none
lines must be a non-empty arraylines is empty
line.defaultColor must be a string
line.defaultWidth must be a number		A line is missing its color or width, or the value has the wrong type
The indicator saves but draws nothingcompute threw an error or ran out of time, or the result has the wrong shape (line order or values length)

callout.title: Build it in small steps
callout.body: Errors during a calculation are silent, so get the smallest example working first and add to it gradually. To inspect a value, draw it as a temporary extra line and read it in the legend.

success: The smallest example appears on the chart after saving.
You can explain what compute receives and returns.
You know where to look when an indicator saves but draws nothing.

faq.q: Can I use a JavaScript indicator in a trading system or backtest?
faq.a: Not yet. JavaScript indicators draw on charts only; write indicators you want to reference in trading-system rules as TDX formulas.

faq.q: Can I use npm packages or TA-Lib?
faq.a: No. The sandbox has no require or import, so write the calculations in your code. Shared helpers can live inside (() => { … })().

faq.q: When should I use a TDX formula instead?
faq.a: Whenever TDX can express it: it has more than a hundred built-in functions, the editor checks compatibility line by line, it runs faster, and trading-system rules can reference it. JavaScript suits logic TDX cannot express, such as complex loops, multi-step state, or your own algorithms.
console in the sandbox is a placeholder that prints nothing. To inspect a value, draw it as a temporary extra line.
